query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: If a moderate amount (approximately 5–10 at.%) of Al is added to an equiatomic FeCoNi alloy and the material is solution-annealed near 1050 °C followed by rapid quenching, partial B2 ordering or a B2-type secondary phase will form and serve to pin domain walls, raising the coercive field above the ~100 Oe limit observed in single-phase fcc FeCoNi-based alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with fcc structure and a coercive field typically not exceeding ~100 Oe.
generation.intervention: Addition of Al (5–10 at.%) to the FeCoNi alloy, melted and cast via arc melting, followed by solution annealing (e.g., 1050 °C, 2 hours) and quenching.
generation.conditions: Compositions should be prepared by standard arc melting in vacuum or inert atmosphere with appropriate Al addition, then homogenized and solution-annealed at approximately 1050 °C and quenched in water. Room-temperature magnetic measurements are to be performed using VSM or SQUID magnetometry under consistent fields and sample geometries as those used for the single-phase fcc FeCoNi baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a B2-like ordered phase or partially ordered regions within an fcc/bcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Localized ordering or a secondary phase pins domain walls, increasing coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: A coercive field that exceeds 100 Oe while maintaining high saturation magnetization relative to single-phase FeCoNi or closely matched derivatives.
generation.baseline: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a closely related, Al-free derivative with a coercive field consistently below 100 Oe.
generation.boundary: Intervention tested in the Al composition range of about 5–10 at.%. Excessive Al additions or different heat-treatment protocols may form other phases or degrade bulk properties, requiring careful tuning of composition and processing.
generation.uncertainty: While an elevated coercivity is expected, the precise magnitude depends on the Al concentration and heat-treatment parameters; mechanical trade-offs require further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce baseline (Al-free) and Al-doped (5%, 10%, 15% Al) FeCoNi alloys by arc melting. Homogenize and solution-anneal at 1050 °C for 2 hours, followed by rapid quenching. Characterize the crystal structure using XRD/TEM to confirm partial B2 ordering and measure magnetic properties by VSM/SQUID at room temperature.
measurements: X-ray diffraction and microstructural analysis to identify B2 or secondary phase development
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed Al-doped alloys do not exceed 100 Oe in coercive field or show no evidence of partial B2 ordering versus the Al-free baseline, the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, the magnetic properties of HEAs with varying composition have been extensively investigated. The CuAl contents had obvious influence on the microstructure and saturation magnetization of FeCoNi(CuAl)x alloy, and the Ms of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 alloy increased from 78.9 Am2 kg−1 to 93.1 Am2 kg−1 by annealing at 673 K. Annealing can effectively improve the saturation magnetization of a certain constituent. Zhang et al. have prepared the FeCoNi(SiAl)x HEAs by arc-melting method and found that the electrical resistivity increased and sacrificed the magnetization with adding SiAl content, and the coercivity with a single-phase structure (BCC or FCC) was smaller than that of the two-phase structure (BCC and FCC). Therefore, the alloy components and annealing process have great influence on the magnetic properties of alloys. In addition, Chen et al. found that the electrical conductivity of FeCoNiCrAlx alloys decreased as x increasing in single-phase (FCC or BCC) regions and the electrical conductivity in duplex phase region possessed smaller value than that in single region.
